task.goal: Diagnose intermittent vibration in one of six identical ventilation fans before a planned maintenance shutdown.
hard_constraints: A mechanic has one week, a handheld vibration meter, existing maintenance logs and one 30-minute shutdown window.
Do not open energized housings or stop all ventilation simultaneously.
Distinguish imbalance, loose mounting and bearing wear without claiming a cause from one noisy measurement; state a safe escalation trigger.
task.available_resources: Five healthy fans as comparators and a spare mounting kit.
task.expected_result: A prioritized diagnostic sequence and repair decision.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Matched-condition comparison before targeted shutdown inspection
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: distinguish a persistent mechanical signature from operating-condition effects by repeatedly comparing the suspect fan with the five healthy units. Assumptions: external bearing supports and mounting points are safely accessible, operating conditions can be identified, and the meter supports repeatable readings. Frequency or bearing-condition features are optional; a basic overall-value meter cannot reliably separate imbalance from bearing wear alone.

During the first four days, review logs for onset, prior bearing or mounting work, and links to speed or ventilation demand. Measure all six fans at equivalent external locations, in the same directions, using consistent meter contact and settings. Repeat across several operating periods, recording load or speed when available. Prioritize inspection when the suspect repeatedly exceeds the healthy range under comparable conditions. Strong radial vibration with a rotational-frequency component, if measurable, supports imbalance; visible mounting movement or inconsistent directional response supports looseness; bearing-localized vibration, roughness, or supported high-frequency indications support bearing wear. None establishes a cause alone.

Use the 30-minute window to isolate and lock out only the suspect fan, after confirming the remaining ventilation is adequate. Prioritize external mounting inspection, then accessible bearing play and roughness checks, then safe visual inspection for blade damage or deposits. Install the spare mounting kit only where compatible and warranted, using specified torque. Do not attempt unsupported balancing or a rushed bearing replacement. If evidence favors imbalance or bearing wear, arrange the appropriate specialist repair.

Escalate immediately under site procedures for rapid worsening, severe knocking, visible structural movement, rubbing, or an applicable equipment alarm limit. Stop and isolate the affected fan when required; preserve other ventilation. Missing limits or inconsistent evidence require engineering review rather than a confident diagnosis.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Smallest check: repeat matched readings on the suspect and one healthy fan before and after any repair, at unchanged locations and comparable operation. If their ranges overlap or the suspected signature does not repeat, the initial diagnosis is unsupported. Improvement after mounting repair supports a mounting contribution; persistent vibration requires further investigation. Record uncertainty and retain both comparison records.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use the shutdown as a controlled mounting intervention
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: use a documented mounting correction as a causal intervention, rather than relying chiefly on vibration signatures. This is useful when the handheld meter measures only overall vibration. Prerequisites are a compatible spare mounting kit, approved mounting and torque instructions, safe external measurement points, and confirmation that five operating fans can maintain required ventilation. The method can identify a mounting contribution but cannot conclusively distinguish imbalance from bearing wear without additional evidence.

Early in the week, review maintenance logs and collect repeated suspect-fan readings alongside one healthy comparator, checking the other healthy fans to establish normal variation. Keep measurement position, direction, settings, and operating condition consistent. Document externally visible mounting defects without touching moving parts or opening energized housings. Prepare tools, kit, isolation arrangements, and a time-limited work plan before the shutdown.

During the single 30-minute window, isolate and lock out only the suspect fan. First inspect and document mounting condition. Check accessible bearing roughness or play and inspect the rotor for deposits, damage, or rubbing where safely possible. If a mounting defect is present, correct it with the spare kit and specified torque. Avoid unrelated adjustments so the intervention remains interpretable. If mounting is sound, do not replace it merely to create an experiment: use the remaining time for inspection and plan the indicated repair. Restore guards before restart; leave the fan isolated if safe restoration cannot be completed.

A sustained reduction after correction supports looseness as a contributor. Residual vibration associated with rotor deposits or damage favors an imbalance investigation; bearing roughness or abnormal play favors bearing service. Either can coexist with looseness. Inconclusive residual vibration warrants specialist diagnostics, not a forced choice.

Escalate immediately for rapid vibration growth, severe knocking, rubbing, structural movement, or an applicable alarm limit. Follow site isolation procedures while maintaining the other ventilation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare several pre-intervention and post-intervention readings with the unchanged healthy fan under matched operation. A reduction larger than ordinary repeat variation, sustained on subsequent checks, supports the mounting hypothesis. No reduction weakens mounting as the principal cause. A simultaneous change in the healthy comparator suggests operating-condition confounding; defer the repair conclusion until matched readings are available.

EXPAND.title: Use the planned coast-down to expose speed-dependent vibration
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: observe how vibration changes as the suspect fan slows during its already planned shutdown. A repeatable peak confined to part of the coast-down suggests speed-dependent structural amplification, which can mislead steady-running comparisons. This adds evidence for separating imbalance, loose mounting and bearing wear; it cannot uniquely identify them.

Prerequisites: the fan must coast freely long enough for the meter to resolve changes, with a safely accessible external measurement point. No speed sweep, extra shutdown or additional instrument is required. Without speed measurement, elapsed time is only a rough indicator of decreasing speed.

During the week, the mechanic reviews logs and repeats matched readings on all six fans, recording operating conditions and whether intermittent episodes recur. Select the suspect’s strongest repeatable external measurement location. Prepare isolation, compatible mounting parts, torque instructions and inspection tools before the window. Confirm that the other five fans can maintain required ventilation.

At the planned stop, keep the meter at that location and record successive readings through coast-down from outside guards. Apply full lockout and verify zero motion before inspection. Within the remaining window, inspect mounting joints, accessible bearing play or roughness, and rotor deposits or damage. A narrow coast-down peak warrants investigation of mounting or structural resonance rather than automatic balancing. Repeated running vibration plus rotor defects supports an imbalance investigation; damaged mounting joints support mounting repair; abnormal bearing play or roughness supports bearing service. Multiple faults remain possible.

Use the spare kit only for a confirmed compatible mounting repair. Restore guards before restart; leave the suspect isolated if safe restoration cannot finish. Escalate immediately for rapid worsening, severe knocking, rubbing, structural movement or an applicable alarm limit, preserving required ventilation. Unresolved evidence goes to specialist diagnosis.
EXPAND.experiment: The mechanic owns one trial during the single window. Before stopping, record the provisional decision from steady-running comparisons alone; then assess whether coast-down and inspection change that decision with corroborating evidence. Stop coast-down recording if it delays isolation or inspection. Compare diagnostic usefulness and inspection time lost: if the transient is too short, indistinct or uncorroborated, this route offers no demonstrated improvement over the prior comparison-and-inspection route. After any repair, repeat matched running readings; persistent vibration triggers handoff rather than another speculative repair.

EXPAND.title: Improved P0: matched-condition comparison with a shutdown readiness gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Source mechanism: P0’s repeated comparison followed by targeted inspection. The improvement is to reserve the limited shutdown for an executable inspection or repair, with explicit fallback decisions when access, tools or ventilation capacity are inadequate. This changes how evidence becomes a maintenance decision; superiority is untested.

During days 1–4, the mechanic reviews logs and measures equivalent safely accessible external points on all six fans, using consistent directions, contact and meter settings. Repeat during several operating periods, recording known speed or demand and capturing intermittent episodes where possible. Healthy fans establish contextual variation, not a universal safety limit. A basic overall vibration meter cannot identify imbalance or bearing wear by itself.

Before the window, verify isolation arrangements, adequate ventilation with the suspect stopped, inspection access, compatible mounting parts, specified torque and availability of required tools. Plan only work that can be safely completed within 30 minutes, including restoration. If tools or access are unavailable, use the window for accessible inspection and hand off the repair. If remaining ventilation is inadequate, arrange an approved ventilation contingency before stopping the suspect; otherwise escalate the scheduling constraint.

During the window, isolate and lock out only the suspect and verify zero motion. Inspect mounting joints first, then accessible bearing play or roughness and rotor deposits or damage. Repair documented mounting defects with the compatible kit and specified torque. Rotor defects support an imbalance investigation; bearing roughness or abnormal play supports bearing service. Neither absence of play nor a single reading clears a bearing. Multiple faults remain possible.

Restore guards before restart and repeat matched measurements. Leave the fan isolated if safe restoration cannot finish. Rapid worsening, severe knocking, rubbing, structural movement or an applicable alarm limit triggers immediate site escalation and affected-fan isolation as required, while maintaining required ventilation.
EXPAND.experiment: The mechanic owns one week-long trial. Compare against P0 using the same readings: record whether the readiness gate changes the work decision, enables completion within 30 minutes, or prevents an unsupported restart; also record preparation time. After any mounting repair, compare repeated readings with its baseline and healthy-fan variation. If the gate changes nothing and only adds work, no practical gain is demonstrated. Stop work at the preallocated restoration deadline or immediately on an escalation trigger.

EXPAND.title: Use the stopped fan to test whether vibration is transmitted from elsewhere
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: make the suspect fan a stationary receiver during its existing shutdown. Vibration that persists after verified zero rotation must have an external excitation component. This can prevent a mistaken local repair when intermittent vibration travels through shared supports or ductwork. It does not exclude a concurrent local defect or identify the external source by itself.

During the week, the mechanic reviews logs for episodes associated with other fans or ventilation demand. Collect repeated readings at safely accessible suspect bearing supports and its supporting structure, plus equivalent locations on healthy fans. Record operating conditions and meter settings. Prepare compatible mounting parts, approved torque information, necessary tools and isolation arrangements. Confirm that the five remaining fans can maintain required ventilation.

At the single shutdown, record running readings at selected external points. Isolate and lock out only the suspect; verify zero motion, including protection against windmilling. With other ventilation continuing, spend at most three minutes repeating readings at the same points and settings. Compare only readings with sufficiently similar remaining-system conditions. Persistent vibration clearly above meter repeatability supports transmission; a large decrease supports a local rotating contribution. Neither result distinguishes imbalance from bearing wear alone. If the meter cannot resolve the stopped readings, treat the test as inconclusive and proceed directly to inspection.

Use the remaining window to inspect mounting joints, accessible bearing roughness or play, and rotor deposits or damage. A mounting defect warrants a compatible, time-feasible repair. Rotor defects plus a local rotating contribution support imbalance investigation; bearing roughness or abnormal play supports bearing service. Persistent stationary vibration with sound local inspections warrants investigation of shared supports, ductwork or neighboring equipment before speculative local replacement.

Restore guards and repeat measurements after a safe restart; otherwise retain isolation and hand off. Escalate immediately for rapid worsening, severe knocking, rubbing, structural movement or an applicable alarm limit. Maintain required ventilation throughout.
EXPAND.experiment: The mechanic owns a first trial within the existing window. Before stopping, record the provisional repair decision from running comparisons alone. Add the stationary readings, then document whether they change that decision and how much inspection time they consume. Compare running, stopped and restored-running readings where operating conditions permit. Negligible stopped vibration provides no support for transmission; failure to change the decision demonstrates no immediate decision benefit. End this test after three minutes, sooner if isolation or ventilation conditions are uncertain; preserve restoration time and escalate unsafe findings.
